messages.subject: modelling a mixture of functions
parts:
Dear all -

I'm trying to model my data as a baseline plus mixture of three functions: Gaussian, linear, and a two-segment function. I've used the code from stagnant data to model a two-segment function and the examples from finite mixture in the manual to set up the model. However, the results with simulated data are still far from truth, so I'm probably doing something wrong.

Here's the R code for the data:
c_avg = 5

bp_u = 30
c_u = c(1, -1)
beta_u = c(0, -0.02)

beta_lin = -0.03

beta_g = 80
sigma_g = 30

fracs = c(1/3, 1/3, 1/3)

set.seed(1)
x<-runif(200,0,90)

y1 <- (x < bp_u)*(c_u[1]+beta_u[1]*x) + (x >= bp_u)*(c_u[2]+beta_u[2]*x)

y2 <- beta_lin*x

y3 <- (beta_g*(1/sigma_g*sqrt(2*pi))*exp(-(x^2)/(2*(sigma_g^2))))

set.seed(1)
y <- c_avg+fracs[1]*y1 + fracs[2]*y2 + fracs[3]*y3+rnorm(200,0,0.1)

And here's the model:

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  real x[N];
  real Y[N];
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0> sigma;
 
  real c_avg;
 
  real c_u[2];
  real beta_u[2];
  real<lower=min(x),upper=max(x)> bp_u;
 
  real beta_lin;
 
  real beta_g;
  real<lower=0> sigma_g;

  simplex[3] fracs;
}

model {
  real mu[N];
  real log_probs[3];
 
  fracs ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(1.0/3.0,3));
 
  c_avg  ~ normal(0,100);
 
  c_u  ~ normal(0,100);
  beta_u ~ normal(0,100);
  beta_lin ~ normal(0,100);
  sigma_g ~ cauchy(0,100);
  sigma ~ cauchy(0,5);
 
  for (k in 1:3){
    for (n in 1:N){
      if (k==1)
        mu[n] <- fracs[1]*(c_avg+(x[n] < bp_u)*(c_u[1]+beta_u[1]*(x[n]-bp_u)) + (x[n] >= bp_u)*(c_u[2]+beta_u[2]*(x[n]-bp_u)));
      else if (k==2)
        mu[n] <- fracs[2]*(c_avg+beta_lin*x[n]);
      else if (k==3)
        mu[n] <- fracs[3]*(c_avg+beta_g*(1/sigma_g*sqrt(2*pi()))*exp(-(x[n]^2)/(2*(sigma_g^2))));
    }
    log_probs[k] <- log(fracs[k]) + normal_log(Y, mu, sigma);
  }
  increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log_probs));
}

Here's the result with 3 chains:

My first guess is that I'm doing something wrong with the constant term (c_avg).  But I'm new to Bayesian analysis and probably there are other things that are wrong too, so I'll be very grateful for your help.

Best,
Andrey Chetverikov

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] modelling a mixture of functions
parts:
Andrey, sorry for missing your follow up questions.

Bob, thanks for following up.

Part of the problem is that we don't know your intention. What do you mean by n-segment function?


Daniel

> On Apr 7, 2016, at 5:47 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> Sorry we're slowing down in replies. I'm trying to catch us up.
>
> I couldn't understand the intent of that function from looking
> at it and am not patient enough to go through it index by index,
> I'm afraid.
>
> If it's a mixture, I don't know why fracs is in two places.
> They wouldn't normally appear in the expression for mu.
>
> - Bob
>
>> On Mar 17, 2016, at 10:09 AM, Andrey Chetverikov <stop...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> Hi Daniel -
>>
>> Sorry for not being clear. The question is, am I specifying the model correctly? If I do, then why the results are not accurate?
>>
>> Best,
>> Andrey
>>
>> On Thursday, 17 March 2016, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
>> Hi Andrey,
>>
>> Sorry -- I just reread your post a couple times. What's your question?
>>
>>
>> Daniel
>>
>>
>> On Tuesday, March 15, 2016 at 4:20:48 PM UTC-4, Andrey Chetverikov wrote:
>> Dear all -
>>
>> I'm trying to model my data as a baseline plus mixture of three functions: Gaussian, linear, and a two-segment function. I've used the code from stagnant data to model a two-segment function and the examples from finite mixture in the manual to set up the model. However, the results with simulated data are still far from truth, so I'm probably doing something wrong.
>>
>> Here's the R code for the data:
>> c_avg = 5
>>
>> bp_u = 30
>> c_u = c(1, -1)
>> beta_u = c(0, -0.02)
>>
>> beta_lin = -0.03
>>
>> beta_g = 80
>> sigma_g = 30
>>
>> fracs = c(1/3, 1/3, 1/3)
>>
>> set.seed(1)
>> x<-runif(200,0,90)
>>
>> y1 <- (x < bp_u)*(c_u[1]+beta_u[1]*x) + (x >= bp_u)*(c_u[2]+beta_u[2]*x)
>>
>> y2 <- beta_lin*x
>>
>> y3 <- (beta_g*(1/sigma_g*sqrt(2*pi))*exp(-(x^2)/(2*(sigma_g^2))))
>>
>> set.seed(1)
>> y <- c_avg+fracs[1]*y1 + fracs[2]*y2 + fracs[3]*y3+rnorm(200,0,0.1)
>>
>> And here's the model:
>>
>> data {
>> int<lower=0> N;
>> real x[N];
>> real Y[N];
>> }
>> parameters {
>> real<lower=0> sigma;
>>
>> real c_avg;
>>
>> real c_u[2];
>> real beta_u[2];
>> real<lower=min(x),upper=max(x)> bp_u;
>>
>> real beta_lin;
>>
>> real beta_g;
>> real<lower=0> sigma_g;
>>
>> simplex[3] fracs;
>> }
>>
>> model {
>> real mu[N];
>> real log_probs[3];
>>
>> fracs ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(1.0/3.0,3));
>>
>> c_avg ~ normal(0,100);
>>
>> c_u ~ normal(0,100);
>> beta_u ~ normal(0,100);
>> beta_lin ~ normal(0,100);
>> sigma_g ~ cauchy(0,100);
>> sigma ~ cauchy(0,5);
>>
>> for (k in 1:3){
>> for (n in 1:N){
>> if (k==1)
>> mu[n] <- fracs[1]*(c_avg+(x[n] < bp_u)*(c_u[1]+beta_u[1]*(x[n]-bp_u)) + (x[n] >= bp_u)*(c_u[2]+beta_u[2]*(x[n]-bp_u)));
>> else if (k==2)
>> mu[n] <- fracs[2]*(c_avg+beta_lin*x[n]);
>> else if (k==3)
>> mu[n] <- fracs[3]*(c_avg+beta_g*(1/sigma_g*sqrt(2*pi()))*exp(-(x[n]^2)/(2*(sigma_g^2))));
>> }
>> log_probs[k] <- log(fracs[k]) + normal_log(Y, mu, sigma);
>> }
>> increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log_probs));
>> }
>>
>> Here's the result with 3 chains:
>> $summary
>> mean se_mean sd 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 98% n_eff Rhat
>> sigma 0.31 7.4e-02 9.2e-02 1.7e-01 0.188 0.36 0.38 4.1e-01 1.5 6.4
>> c_avg 65.20 1.1e+01 5.9e+01 4.3e+00 17.922 45.65 101.37 2.2e+02 29.3 1.1
>> c_u[1] 0.76 2.6e+00 9.9e+01 -1.9e+02 -66.990 0.23 70.90 2.0e+02 1500.0 1.0
>> c_u[2] -2.45 2.7e+00 9.9e+01 -2.0e+02 -69.807 -1.60 62.75 1.9e+02 1327.0 1.0
>> beta_u[1] -6.41 2.6e+00 9.9e+01 -2.0e+02 -69.214 -8.17 60.04 1.9e+02 1500.0 1.0
>> beta_u[2] -1.28 2.7e+00 1.0e+02 -2.0e+02 -71.444 -0.38 68.01 2.0e+02 1500.0 1.0
>> bp_u 45.48 6.5e-01 2.5e+01 3.9e+00 23.939 44.81 66.46 8.8e+01 1500.0 1.0
>> beta_lin -0.12 1.4e+00 5.5e+01 -1.4e+02 -1.095 -0.39 -0.12 1.5e+02 1500.0 1.0
>> beta_g 4181.74 4.4e+03 1.3e+04 -2.5e+04 98.256 1676.40 9122.49 3.3e+04 9.1 1.7
>> sigma_g 247.68 7.9e+01 8.5e+02 5.9e+00 28.979 40.61 160.52 1.4e+03 117.9 1.0

>>
>> My first guess is that I'm doing something wrong with the constant term (c_avg). But I'm new to Bayesian analysis and probably there are other things that are wrong too, so I'll be very grateful for your help.
